questions.q: A liquid is kept in a glass beaker. Which one of the following statements is correct regarding the pressure exerted by the liquid column at the base of the beaker?
options: The pressure depends on the area of the base of the beaker
The pressure depends on the height of liquid column
The pressure does not depend on the density of the liquid
The pressure neither depends on the area of the base of the beaker nor on the height of liquid column
questions.solution: The pressure of liquid kept in a glass beaker depends upon the height of liquid column inside the beaker. Pressure at different heights from the surface of liquid is given by formula, $\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{A}}+\rho \mathrm{gh}$ Where, $P$ is total pressure, $\rho=$ density of liquid, $g$ is acceleration due to gravity and h is height of the liquid from the surface.

questions.q:
Two equal resistors R are connected in parallel, and a battery of 12 V is connected across this combination. A dc current of 100 mA flows through the circuit as shown below:
The value of $R$ is
questions.solution:
Let R' be the equivalent resistance of two resistors.
As they are connected in parallel
$\begin{aligned}
& \frac{1}{R^{\prime}}=\frac{1}{R}+\frac{1}{R} \\
& R^{\prime}=\frac{R}{2} (i)
\end{aligned}$
Using ohm's law
$V=I R^{\prime}\begin{aligned}
& R^{\prime}=\frac{V}{I}=\frac{12}{100 \times 10^{-3}} \\
& \Rightarrow \mathrm{R}^{\prime}=120 \Omega
\end{aligned}$
But, $R^{\prime}=\frac{R}{2}\therefore \quad \mathrm{R}=2 \times \mathrm{R}^{\prime}=2 \times 120=240 \Omega$

According to Kepler's law of planetary motion, $\mathrm{T}^2 \propto \mathrm{R}^3$
Therefore, the ratio of the time period is given by,
$\begin{aligned}
& \frac{T_1^2}{T_2^2}=\frac{R^3}{(4 R)^3}=\frac{1}{64} \\
& \Rightarrow \frac{T_1}{T_2}=\frac{1}{8}
\end{aligned}$
i.e., $T_1: T_2$ is $1: 8$

Longitudinal Waves: A wave in which the particles of the medium vibrate back and forth in the 'same direction' in which the wave is moving. Medium can be solid, liquid or gases. Therefore, sound waves are longitudinal waves. Sound is a longitudinal wave which consists of compressions and rarefactions travelling through a medium.
Transverse Waves: A wave in which the particles of the medium vibrate up and down 'at right angles' to the direction in which the wave is moving. These waves are produced only in a solids and liquids but not in gases.

Area, $A=l \cdot b=\frac{K}{2} \cdot \frac{K}{2}=\frac{K^2}{4}$

Consider the following statements for $f(x)=e^{-|x|}$ :

2. The function is differentiable at $x=0$. Which of the above statements is/are correct?

(1) $f(x)=e^{-|x|}, f(0)=e^{-|0|}=1$.
$\begin{gathered}
f(x)=e^{-x}, \text { for } x \geq 0 \\
=e^x, \quad \text { for } x \lt 0
\end{gathered}\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{LHL}=\lim _{x \rightarrow 0^{-}} f(x)=\lim _{x \rightarrow 0^{-}} e^x=1 \\ & \mathrm{RHL}=\lim _{x \rightarrow 0^{+}} f(x)=\lim _{x \rightarrow 0^{+}} e^{-x}=1\end{aligned}$
As,$f(0)=\mathrm{LHL}=\mathrm{RHL}$
Thus $f(x)$ is continuous at $x=0$.
(2) $\mathrm{LHD}=\lim _{x \rightarrow 0^{-}} f^{\prime}(x)=\lim _{x \rightarrow 0^{-}} e^x=e^0=1\mathrm{RHD}=\lim _{x \rightarrow 0^{+}} f^{\prime}(x)=\lim _{x \rightarrow 0^{+}}-e^{-x}=-e^0=-1$
As LHD \neq  RHD
Hence, $f(x)$ is not differentiable at $x=0$.

questions.q: If $\lim _{x \rightarrow 1} \frac{x^4-1}{x-1}=\lim _{x \rightarrow k} \frac{x^3-k^3}{x^2-k^2}$, where $k \neq 0$, then what is the value of $k$ ?
questions.solution:
$\begin{aligned}
\lim _{x \rightarrow 1} \frac{x^4-1}{x-1} & =\lim _{x \rightarrow 1} \frac{(x-1)(x+1)\left(x^2+1\right)}{(x-1)} \\
& =\lim _{x \rightarrow 1}(x+1)\left(x^2+1\right)=(1+1)(1+1)=4
\end{aligned}$
Now, $\lim _{x \rightarrow k} \frac{x^3-k^3}{x^2-k^2}=4\lim _{x \rightarrow k} \frac{(x-k)\left(x^2+k^2+x k\right)}{(x-k)(x+k)}=4\begin{aligned} & \lim _{x \rightarrow k} \frac{\left(x^2+k^2+x k\right)}{(x+k)}=4 \\ & \frac{k^2+k^2+k \cdot k}{k+k}=4 \Rightarrow \frac{3}{2} k=4 \Rightarrow k=\frac{8}{3}\end{aligned}$

questions.q: If $P(A \cup B)=\frac{5}{6}, P(A \cap B)=\frac{1}{3}$ and $P(\operatorname{not} A)=\frac{1}{2}$, then which one of the following is not correct?
options: $P(\operatorname{not} A$ and $\operatorname{not} B)=P(\operatorname{not} A) P(\operatorname{not} B)$
questions.solution:
$\begin{aligned}
& P(A \cup B)=\frac{5}{6}, P(A \cap B)=\frac{1}{3}, P\left(A^{\prime}\right)=\frac{1}{2} \\
& P(A)=1-P\left(A^{\prime}\right)=1-\frac{1}{2}=\frac{1}{2} \\
& P(A \cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A \cap B)
\end{aligned}\frac{5}{6}=\frac{1}{2}+P(B)-\frac{1}{3}$
(a) $P(B)=\frac{5}{6}-\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{3}=\frac{5-3+2}{6}=\frac{4}{6}=\frac{2}{3}$
(b) $P(A \cap B)=\frac{1}{3}=\frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{2}{3}=P(A) \cdot P(B)\therefore P(A \cap B)=P(A) \cdot P(B)$
(c) $P(A \cup B)=\frac{5}{6}\begin{aligned}
& P(A)+P(B)=\frac{1}{2}+\frac{2}{3}=\frac{7}{6} \\
& \therefore P(A \cup B) \lt P(A)+P(B)
\end{aligned}$
Hence, option (c) is not correct.
(d) $P\left(A^{\prime} \cap B^{\prime}\right)=P\left(A^{\prime}\right) \cdot P\left(B^{\prime}\right)\begin{aligned} & 1-P(A \cup B)=1-\frac{5}{6}=\frac{1}{6} \\ & \text {and } P\left(A^{\prime}\right) \cdot P\left(B^{\prime}\right)=(1-P(A)) \cdot(1-P(B)) \\ & =\left(1-\frac{1}{2}\right) \cdot\left(1-\frac{2}{3}\right)=\frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{1}{3}=\frac{1}{6}\end{aligned}$
Hence, $P\left(A^{\prime} \cap B^{\prime}\right)=P\left(A^{\prime}\right) \cdot P\left(B^{\prime}\right)$.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: The roots $\alpha$ and $\beta$ of a quadratic equation, satisfy the relations $\alpha+\beta=\alpha^2+\beta^2$ and $\alpha \beta=\alpha^2 \beta^2$. What is the number of such quadratic equations?
questions.solution:
$\begin{aligned}
&  \alpha \beta=\alpha^2 \beta^2 \Rightarrow \alpha \beta(1-\alpha \beta)=0 \\
& \therefore \alpha \beta=0 \text { or } 1
\end{aligned}$
When $\alpha \beta=1$ then $\alpha=\frac{1}{\beta}\begin{aligned} & \text { Again from } \alpha+\beta=\alpha^2+\beta^2 \\ & \Rightarrow \frac{1}{\beta}+\beta=\frac{1}{\beta^2}+\beta^2 \Rightarrow \beta^2-\beta=\frac{1}{\beta}-\frac{1}{\beta^2} \\ & \Rightarrow \beta(\beta-1)=\frac{(\beta-1)}{\beta^2} \Rightarrow(\beta-1)\left(\beta-\frac{1}{\beta^2}\right)=0\end{aligned}\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow(\beta-1)\left(\beta^3-1\right)=0 \Rightarrow(\beta-1)^2\left(\beta^2+\beta+1\right)=0 \\ & \therefore \beta=1 \text { and } \beta=\frac{-1 \pm \sqrt{3} i}{2}\end{aligned}$
Again, when $\beta=1$, then $\alpha=\frac{1}{\beta}=1$, roots $(\alpha, \beta)=(1,1)$ When $\beta=\frac{-1+\sqrt{3} i}{2}$, then $\alpha=\frac{-1-\sqrt{3} i}{2}$
Roots $(\alpha, \beta)=\left(\frac{-1 \pm \sqrt{3} i}{2}, \frac{-1 \mp \sqrt{3} i}{2}\right)$
Thus, number of different quadratic equations $=2$.

questions.q: What is the standard deviation of the observations $-\sqrt{6},-\sqrt{5},-\sqrt{4},-1,1, \sqrt{4}, \sqrt{5}, \sqrt{6}$ ?

$\bar{x}=\frac{\text { Sum of datas }}{\text { Number of data }}=0\begin{aligned} & (x-\bar{x})^2=(-\sqrt{6}-0)^2+(-\sqrt{5}-0)^2+(-\sqrt{4}-0)^2+ \\ & (-1-0)^2+(1-0)^2+(\sqrt{4}-0)^2+(\sqrt{5}-0)^2+(\sqrt{6}-0)^2 \\ & =6+5+4+1+1+4+5+6=32 \\ & \text {S.D. }=\sqrt{\frac{(x-\bar{x})^2}{N}}=\sqrt{\frac{32}{8}}=\sqrt{4}=2\end{aligned}$

questions.q: If a line has direction ratios $\lt  a+b, b+c, c+a  \gt $, then what is the sum of the squares of its direction cosines?
questions.solution:
Direction ratios are $ \lt a+b, b+c, c+a \gt $ Then, direction cosine,
$\begin{aligned} & l=\frac{(a+b)}{\sqrt{(a+b)^2+(b+c)^2+(c+a)^2}} \\ & m=\frac{(b+c)}{\sqrt{(a+b)^2+(b+c)^2+(c+a)^2}}\end{aligned}n=\frac{(c+a)}{\sqrt{(a+b)^2+(b+c)^2+(c+a)^2}}$
Sum of squares of direction cosines
$l^2+m^2+n^2=\frac{(a+b)^2+(b+c)^2+(c+a)^2}{(a+b)^2+(b+c)^2+(c+a)^2}=1$

Let $A=(x, y, z)$

$y=|O A| \cdot \cos 60^{\circ}=12 \cdot \frac{1}{2}=6 \hat{j}$
Hence, $\overrightarrow{O A}=6 \sqrt{2} \hat{i}+6 \hat{j} \pm 6 \hat{k}$

Paragraph: Read the following information and answer: $A B C D$ is a trapezium such that $A B$ and $C D$ are parallel and $B C$ is perpendicular to them. Let $\angle A D B=\theta, \angle A B D=\alpha, B C=p$ and $C D=q$ and $C D=q$.

From $\triangle A B D$,
$\begin{aligned}
& \frac{A B}{\sin \theta}=\frac{B D}{\sin \left(180^{\circ}-(\alpha+\theta)\right)} \\
& \Rightarrow A B=\frac{B D \cdot \sin \theta}{\sin (\alpha+\theta)}=\frac{B D \cdot \sin \theta}{\sin \alpha \cdot \cos \theta+\cos \alpha \cdot \sin \theta}
\end{aligned}$
Again from $\triangle B C D$,
$\begin{aligned} & B D=\sqrt{(B C)^2+(C D)^2}=\sqrt{p^2+q^2} \\ & \sin \alpha=\frac{B C}{B D}=\frac{p}{\sqrt{p^2+q^2}} \\ & \cos \alpha=\frac{C D}{B D}=\frac{q}{\sqrt{p^2+q^2}}\end{aligned}\begin{aligned} \therefore A B & =\frac{\sqrt{p^2+q^2} \cdot \sin \theta}{\frac{p \cdot \cos \theta}{\sqrt{p^2+q^2}}+\frac{q \cdot \sin \theta}{\sqrt{p^2+q^2}}} \\ & =\frac{\left(p^2+q^2\right) \cdot \sin \theta}{p \cdot \cos \theta+q \cdot \sin \theta}\end{aligned}$
